summary: Defines a new iss parameter that carries the authorization server's issuer identifier in the OAuth authorization response. It is a countermeasure to mix-up attacks, in which a client is tricked about which authorization server is responding. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a reply comes back, it says who sent it, so a trickster cannot pretend to be someone else.

questions: what is an oauth mix-up attack
what does the iss parameter do in oauth
subtitle: A one-parameter fix that lets an OAuth client check which authorization server actually sent a response.

tldr.problem: An OAuth authorization response does not say which authorization server issued it, so a client that talks to several servers can be tricked into sending an authorization code or access token to an attacker (a mix-up attack).
tldr.mechanism: The authorization server adds an iss parameter holding its issuer identifier to every authorization response, including errors, and the client compares it to the issuer it believes it is talking to.
tldr.outcome: A client that validates iss rejects responses from the wrong server, which defends against mix-up attacks. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: iss value
facts.value: https URL, no query or fragment

today: RFC 9207 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Mix-Up Attack Problem
sections.content:
The OAuth 2.0 framework (RFC 6749) lets a client work with several independent authorization servers. Some grant types, such as the authorization code grant, send the server's answer to the client through the resource owner's user agent. That answer does not say which server issued it.

Because of this, the client cannot be sure who produced the response and the secrets inside it. This enables mix-up attacks. If at least one of the servers a client supports is controlled by an attacker, the attacker can try to obtain authorization codes or access tokens issued by any of the other servers. The attacker might control a server because it was compromised, or because the attacker registered their own, for example using dynamic client registration (RFC 7591).

A client that talks to only one authorization server is not vulnerable. If it later adds a second server, it becomes vulnerable and needs a countermeasure.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine getting a sealed letter with no return address. If a bad person is also writing to you, you cannot tell whose letter it is, and you might hand your secret to the wrong one.

sections.title: The iss Response Parameter
sections.content:
An authorization server that supports this specification MUST include the iss parameter in authorization responses to the client, including error responses. Its value is the issuer identifier of the server that created the response, as defined in RFC 8414. The value MUST be a URL with the https scheme and no query or fragment components.

In the RFC's example, a successful redirect to the client carries code, state and iss=https%3A%2F%2Fhonest.as.example. An error redirect carries error=access_denied, state and the same iss.

If the authorization response already carries the issuer in another way, such as an ID Token or the JWT-based JARM mode, the separate iss parameter is not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every reply, even a "no, sorry" reply, gets the sender's web address written on it.

sections.title: How Servers and Clients Use It
sections.content:
A server must make its issuer identifier available so clients can check iss. If it publishes metadata under RFC 8414, the metadata issuer value MUST be identical to the iss value, and the server MUST set the metadata parameter authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported to true. If that parameter is omitted, its default value is false.

A client that supports the specification extracts iss, decodes it from its form-urlencoded form and compares it to the issuer identifier of the server the request was sent to. The comparison MUST be a simple string comparison. On a mismatch the client MUST reject the response and MUST NOT proceed with the grant. For error responses, the client must not assume the error came from the intended server.

Where there is no metadata, clients use deployment-specific ways, such as static configuration, to know the expected value. A client that deals with both supporting and non-supporting servers MUST remember which supports the parameter, and MUST reject responses without iss from servers configured as supporting it. It SHOULD discard responses with iss from servers that do not indicate support. Clients that do not support the specification must ignore the unknown parameter, as RFC 6749 already requires. In OpenID Connect flows that return an ID Token from the authorization endpoint, iss MUST match the iss claim in the token.
sections.plainLanguage: The server writes its name on the reply and tells everyone it does that. You compare the name to the one you expected and throw the letter away if it is different.

sections.title: The Metadata Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC adds one authorization server metadata parameter, authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported. It is a boolean that says whether the server provides iss in its authorization responses. When it is missing, clients treat it as false.

This lets a client learn, before it starts a flow, whether it should expect and require the iss value from that particular server.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a sign on the shop door saying "our letters always have our name on them". If the sign is missing, assume they do not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clients MUST validate iss exactly as described and MUST NOT allow multiple authorization servers to use the same issuer identifier. When server details can be configured by hand, the client must ensure the accepted iss values are unique for each server.

The iss value is not cryptographically protected against tampering. The RFC argues this does not matter for mix-up attacks: the client normally receives the response from an uncompromised server, and an attacker able to tamper with that response would already have direct access to the authorization code, so would not need a mix-up attack.

Other countermeasures exist. If a response already includes the issuer by other means and it is checked as described, using iss may be omitted. If a response contains several issuer identifiers, the client MUST reject it unless they match. The RFC cites a formal analysis that proved the effectiveness of the iss parameter against mix-up attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The name on the envelope could in theory be forged, but anyone who can forge it on the way could already just read your secret, so the name check still does its job against the trick it is designed for.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported in the "OAuth Authorization Server Metadata" registry, with the IETF as change controller and Section 3 of RFC 9207 as the specification.

IANA also updated the existing iss entry in the "OAuth Parameters" registry. Its usage locations are the authorization request and the authorization response, and the specification documents are Section 2 of RFC 9207, RFC 9101 and Section 4.1.1 of RFC 7519.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names were written into the official list of OAuth words so nobody else uses them for something different.
